The ratings map for adidas
Every answer the Investment Analyst wrote in the four layers behind this memo, word for word
The Financial Analyst Memo: every financial table and model output behind this memo
adidas AG (ADS-DE) · Investment memo · 4 November 2026

adidas: about 60% of the 2027 rise in operating profit is already secured, yet the shares trade at 13x earnings; a re-rating to a fair 19.7x would return about 80% by March 2028

Investment Analyst, 4 November 2026. Share price EUR 172.85 (close, 2 November); market value about EUR 29.8bn. Next results: FY2026, with the first FY2027 guidance, on 10 March 2027. Money is in EUR millions unless stated. The sources and the basis of every number are in the end notes.

#0 Summary: the case, the five insights behind it and the two dates that test it

The case in brief. adidas is a well-run, single-brand sportswear company three to four years into a margin recovery. The market prices adidas at about 13x two-year-forward earnings because it reads adidas as a lifestyle brand whose Samba and Gazelle cycle has peaked just as Nike re-arms. Our case is that adidas's 2027 earnings depend far less on that fashion cycle than a 13x multiple implies, for three reasons:

  • About 60% of the 2027 increase in operating profit is locked or semi-locked by dollar hedges, a falling contracted marketing load and season-by-season sourcing contracts.
  • An authorised buyback of EUR 1bn a year fixes the step from net income to EPS.
  • adidas has beaten its initial profit guidance in each of the last four years.

On our forecasts, EPS compounds at about 14% to 16% a year to 2030 while revenue grows only 5.5% to 6% a year, below both consensus and management's ambition. The return therefore does not need an earnings upgrade. The return needs the multiple to stop falling and then to recover part of the way toward the 16x to 20x range at which the stock traded when the market last believed in adidas's compounding.

The five insights that matter most.

  1. 2027 is a margin year on a soft revenue base, and the market has not yet connected the two facts. Our FY2027 EBIT (EUR 2,867m, a 10.0% margin) is within 1% of consensus, but our FY2027 revenue (EUR 28.6bn, +5.5%) is 1.9% below consensus. Lapping the sales from the men's World Cup removes about three points of growth, and footwear sales have been flat for two quarters, so consensus revenue growth of +7.5% is the stretched line and the margin is the secure line. The consensus revision we expect over the next year is a change of composition (revenue down, margin up) with consensus EPS held within a few percent. That revision is neutral for earnings and favourable for the credibility of our case, because it is the pattern our forecasts predict.
  2. Management steers the margin to its target, so adidas's EPS beats will be small and frequent rather than large. Management reinvested half of the 2026 tariff refund and will deliver an operating margin of "about 10%" rather than much above it. The best evidence of momentum therefore sits one line above EBIT, in gross margin and in the marketing and overhead ratios.
  3. The demand leg of the case has an expiry date in mid-2027. Part of adidas's market-share gain since 2024 came from Nike's weakness. Nike's first full new range ships in spring 2027, and Nike's Chinese distributors lose their online rights on 1 January 2027, so external support for adidas's share and gross margin peaks around mid-2027. 2028 carries three dated uncertainties at once: the dollar hedges rolling to new rates, Nike's new ranges in the shops and a second year of decline in the terrace franchises. 2028 is therefore where consensus is most likely to be cut, by 3% to 5% in March 2028 in my central case.
  4. adidas's free cash flow is smaller than the headline consensus figure but still funds the full capital return. Free cash flow after lease payments is about EUR 1.7bn in 2027. The FactSet consensus of EUR 2.0bn to 2.5bn is struck before about EUR 0.75bn a year of lease payments. EUR 1.7bn covers the dividend and the EUR 1bn buyback with EUR 0.2bn to 0.3bn to spare, and the buyback supplies about a fifth of EPS growth in every forecast year.
  5. The model's +183% return to March 2028 at its guideline multiple of 28x should not be assumed. The Master Dashboard's "Reinforcing" phase, and the 90th-percentile multiple attached to that phase, come from a mechanical rule. The fundamentals describe a stock turning up from a de-rating, for which Viewforth's guideline points lower in the range. My fair multiple is 19.7x, the ten-year 35th percentile, which on corrected EPS gives a return of about +80% to March 2028. The 10th percentile (16.3x) gives about +50%, and an unchanged multiple still gives about +20% from EPS growth and dividends. The downside to a fair trough is about -15% to -25%, and it would come from lower earnings, not from a lower multiple.

Five judgements move the share price most (each is sized in #9): footwear growth in 2027; the 2027 gross-margin bridge, specifically whether promotions absorb the hedge gain; how much of any profit surplus management chooses to reinvest; the multiple, which depends on whether the market's concern about Nike passes; and, for 2028, the rates at which the dollar hedges roll.

Two dated events decide the next six months. The first is Nike's investor day on 16 and 17 November 2026: a Nike plan that retailers judge credible for spring 2027 is the risk, and a slow, cautious plan is the positive surprise. The second is the first FY2027 guidance under the incoming CFO on 10 March 2027: a trim to the sales guide with the margin target held would make our composition call explicit, and the market would absorb such a trim within a quarter.

Where I differ from the market. I agree with the street on the level of 2027 profit. I differ on how that profit is made, how predictable it is, how exposed 2028 is, how much cash the business generates and what the low multiple means. The last difference matters for timing: today's multiple is a floor for the whole sportswear group rather than a verdict on adidas alone, so a re-rating needs the group to leave the discount-cycle penalty box as well as adidas to deliver footwear growth.

Scorecard

#1 Operating environment: a 2027 margin tailwind inside a sector-wide volume headwind

Conclusion: the operating environment gives adidas a margin tailwind in 2027 inside a sector-wide volume headwind; the external support peaks around mid-2027, and 2028 is materially less favourable.

Score: 55, set by the Rater. External forces are a front-loaded 2027 margin tailwind (dollar hedges locked at 1.15-1.20 worth about +80bp of gross margin, Nike's reset releasing shelf space, the industry discount cycle ending) set against broad volume headwinds (soft consumer, lifestyle-to-performance rotation hitting the terrace franchises, the World Cup lap, a full year of Section 301 tariffs, freight and cotton); consensus sales growth at the 77th percentile is partly borrowed from Nike and fades in 2028 as Nike's ranges ship and the hedge rolls. A mild net positive, coherent with the group's 54 (supplier bidding is counted in topic 2 as the company's own sourcing action), so above Kerry's neutral 50 but short of OEM's 57 because the support peaks mid-2027.

Evidence. The external forces split cleanly into four company-specific tailwinds, which mostly lift margin, and six broad, cyclical headwinds, which mostly cut volume. The board below sets out each force with its evidence.

Inference. The tailwinds act at company and value-chain level and mostly lift margin; the headwinds act at sector level and mostly cut volume. That split explains why our forecast shows a rising margin and slowing revenue growth at the same time without contradiction. The tailwinds are also front-loaded. The hedge benefit is fully booked by the end of 2027 and may partly reverse in 2028 if the euro weakens toward 1.14 dollars (Morgan Stanley's end-2027 forecast). adidas's window for share gains closes from spring 2027, when Nike's new range ships, although Deutsche Bank expects no Nike sales inflection before Nike's fiscal 2028 (June 2027 to May 2028), and Morgan Stanley's investor-day preview frames a normalised Nike revenue base of only USD 40bn through Nike's fiscal 2031.

So what. External forces are mildly positive for adidas's 2027 earnings, mildly negative for its multiple and less supportive in 2028. The external judgement that most shapes the model is that 2028 revenue growth must not be extrapolated from 2026, because part of adidas's 2025 to 2026 growth was borrowed from Nike's weakness.

Counter-case. A Nike that executes its "Sport Offense" strategy from spring 2027, funded by about USD 2.5bn of cost savings earmarked for demand creation, could reclaim shelf space at full price within two seasons; the Caitlin Clark signature shoe selling out in two hours in October shows that Nike's innovation engine still works. A stronger dollar in 2027 would also flatter adidas's reported revenue while worsening the 2028 hedge roll. What would change my view: retailers describing Nike's spring 2027 pre-orders as rising after the investor day; or Topsports and Pou Sheng, adidas's large Chinese retail partners, restraining adidas orders beyond the first quarter of 2027.

Market view against mine. The sell-side describes every one of these forces but disagrees on their size: broker estimates of the hedge benefit differ by a factor of five, and estimates of the World Cup's sales contribution span a 70% range. I agree with the direction of every force and sit near the middle on size. I differ in dating the support, which I expect to peak in mid-2027, and in treating the 2028 hedge roll, which no broker quantifies, as the largest open external item.

#2 Internal change: the rescue is done, and the next leg is cost, sourcing and buybacks

Conclusion: corporate change at adidas is strong, broad and well funded, but it has moved from rescue to refinement. Its contribution in 2027 and 2028 comes from cost, sourcing and buybacks rather than transformation, and a cost-minded new CFO is the one catalyst that nobody models.

Score: 63, set by the Rater. Change is real, resourced and funded: a proven CEO extended to 2030, overheads below 30% and a margin above 10% targeted for 2028, sourcing worth about 70bp net, EUR 1bn-a-year buybacks taking about 3% of shares a year, and a cost-minded incoming CFO, but the transformation (EBIT EUR 268m to about EUR 2.5bn) is already in the numbers and the next leg is refinement, offset by the CFO/ERP/decentralisation cluster, thin bench and weak governance; the 79th-percentile three-year margin change records the past repair, not the coming leg. Above the group's 60 and Richard's 'gently positive but mediocre' CVS at 55 because the ambition and buyback are concrete, so between OEM's active-acquirer 66 and Odfjell's 61.

Evidence on leadership. adidas's leadership is proven at the top and changing in finance. Bjørn Gulden, CEO since January 2023, has had his contract extended to the end of 2030 and bought EUR 0.5m of shares at EUR 158.93 in July 2026. Harm Ohlmeyer, CFO since 2017 after about 30 years at the company, hands over to Birgit Kretschmer on 1 January 2027. Kretschmer spent 25 years at adidas, including as CFO of Western Europe, where she ran the "ONE Europe" consolidation of five units into one; the regional margin reached 20% in 2015 and 24.4% in the third quarter of 2018, and in 2016 she limited the margin's decline to two points against a three-point gross-margin hit from the dollar. She then spent six years as CFO of C&A Europe, where her record is private; the visible actions at C&A are defensive store closures and 324 lay-offs in France in 2025. Nassef Sawiris, a long-standing large shareholder, became chair of the Supervisory Board in May 2026.

Evidence on strategy, operations and capital returns. In March 2026 management moved the strategy from turnaround to "sustainable brand-led growth", with five targets: high-single-digit currency-neutral growth to 2028; an operating margin of about 10% in 2027 and above 10% in 2028; overheads below 30% of sales by 2028; buybacks of up to EUR 1bn a year in 2027 and 2028 within a leverage ceiling of 2.0x; and a structural 60/40 mix of wholesale and direct sales. Operations have tightened: inventory grew 5% against sales growth of 9.4% in the third quarter, 90% of stock is current or future season, markdowns are 10% to 30% against more than 50% three years ago, 500 headquarters roles were removed in 2025, and EUR 100m is being spent in the fourth quarter of 2026 on legacy IT write-offs and simplification. Capital returns rose to EUR 1.5bn in 2026: a EUR 1bn buyback completed early (6.3m shares at about EUR 159, of which 6.0m were cancelled) and a dividend of EUR 2.80, up 40%.

Evidence on problems. adidas's internal problems are identifiable and centre on control, governance and depth of management:

  • Execution: the second-quarter 2026 cost step-up (marketing at 13.7% of sales, overheads +12%) was badly signalled and cost 12% of the share price in a day; the migration to a new enterprise resource planning (ERP) system delayed shipments; a distributor complained of delays; and former directors describe adidas's demand forecasting as under-developed compared with Nike's.
  • Governance below the standard of a company of adidas's size: shareholders voted against ratifying the Supervisory Board's actions in 2026; the chair is not regarded as independent; a board member was paid EUR 200,000 as a brand ambassador; long-term pay moved to a single performance year; and the CEO's 2024 pay carried a guaranteed minimum variable payout of 80%.
  • A thin bench: procurement reports directly to the CEO, two senior commercial and operations executives left in 2024, and there is no obvious successor to the CEO. The 2027 CFO handover coincides with the ERP roll-out and a decentralisation of regional finance.
  • Rising product complexity: Zalando Germany lists 19,307 adidas products against 13,642 for Nike, as the "wider net" strategy adds sports and lower-priced lines.

Inference. The high-impact changes have already delivered most of their earnings effect: the new CEO, the wholesale reset, the inventory clean-up, the exit from Yeezy and the re-consolidation of suppliers took operating profit from EUR 268m in 2023 to about EUR 2.5bn in 2026. The next leg is narrower and centres on cost, margin and capital returns. The incoming CFO is the one internal catalyst that could add to that next leg. Kretschmer's Western Europe record is a cost-containment record; other recent CFO changes (Nike's Denton, Diageo, Hugo Boss, Puma) produced conservative first guidance followed by tighter cost stories; and a formal overhead programme at the March 2027 results is plausible but modelled by nobody. The invisibility of Kretschmer's C&A record is a gap in the evidence, not a negative.

So what. For the model, the large margin step-changes in the left-hand panel are behind adidas. The remaining internal levers are the four in the middle panel, plus a possible cost programme. Their net effect is positive, but the pace of self-help seen in 2024 and 2025 should not be assumed to continue.

Counter-case. A conservative CFO enforcing cost controls could clash with a growth-first CEO who "will not try to be even more profitable just to impress people". The CFO handover, the ERP roll-out and the decentralisation of finance form a cluster of control risks in the same year. Key-person concentration means that a departure by Gulden would hit the multiple hard, despite his contract running to 2030. What would change my view: a March 2027 guide with no cost message at all; a second shipment disruption caused by the ERP system; or a further governance episode like the brand-ambassador payment.

Market view against mine. The street treats the CFO change as continuity (Deutsche Bank: "unlikely to trigger any strategic shifts") and models no cost programme. I agree that capital allocation will continue unchanged, but I think a cost message is more likely than the street assumes. I treat a cost programme as upside, not as base case.

#3 Business quality: a good business, not a great one, run by an excellent operator

Conclusion: adidas holds a favourable but unstable position in a two-giant industry, with a strong brand, a clean balance sheet, a record gross margin and an excellent operator. Against those strengths stand returns below Nike's, pricing power that rests on brand heat rather than structure, a thin bench and weak governance. adidas is a good business, not a great one, currently delivering at a great business's level.

Score: 62, set by the Rater. One of two mass-scale brands in a deep-profit-pool oligopoly with high barriers to mass entry and an excellent operator (management group 73), but niche entry is easy, shares and competitor pricing are unstable, pricing power is brand heat rather than structure, governance and the bench are weak, and fashion cyclicality lowers predictability (industry 52, advantage 58). The financials are mixed: ROIC 13.3% (78th percentile) and ROE 24% (85th) but sub-Nike, an operating margin at the 31st percentile still recovering only to its 2019 peak, and negative 2025 free cash flow; a good business, not a great one, below Carlsberg's 65 and just above Helios Towers' 60.

Evidence on industry structure. Branded sportswear is an oligopoly of two giants with a profitable but unstable tail of smaller brands. Nike (about EUR 40bn of revenue) and adidas (EUR 24.8bn in FY2025, about EUR 27bn in 2026) are the only brands at mass scale, and Nike's size relative to adidas has fallen from about 2.2 times in 2023 to about 1.6 times. The brand stage holds the deepest profit pool in the value chain: brand gross margins are about 49% against about 21% for contract manufacturers, and brands earn pre-tax returns on capital of about 19%. Barriers to mass scale are high (about EUR 3bn a year of marketing, EUR 7.9bn of athlete, club and federation commitments, and global distribution), but barriers to niche entry are low. On went from 0.1% to 2.1% of global footwear in eight years; Nike's China share fell from 27% to 16% in five years; and adidas itself lost about ten points of China share between 2018 and 2023 before recovering to 10%. Competitors aim to protect margin but clear inventory through promotions when it builds, so industry prices do fall when volume falls.

Every actor in the value chain currently works in adidas's favour: the market leader is in retreat, retailers want full-price product, suppliers compete for volume (Huali's sales to adidas rose more than 50% in the nine months to September), and the discount cycle is ending. Such an alignment is unusual, and it will not last beyond 2027.

Evidence on the business model and moats. adidas's moats keep new mass-scale entrants out but give it a weaker edge over its strongest rivals. Pricing power is demonstrated in practice, yet it rests on brand heat and carries no switching costs. The moats do not yet earn premium returns, and none of them compounds mechanically in the way a network or subscription business does.

Evidence on the financial profile. adidas's gross margin is at a record, but its operating margin is only recovering toward its 2019 peak. Gross margin was 51.6% in FY2025 on the company's basis, about 51.8% underlying in 2026 and 54.3% reported in the third quarter of 2026 including the tariff refund. The operating margin is recovering toward, not beyond, the 2019 peak (company basis 11.3%; FactSet adjusted 10.9%), because marketing of about 12% of sales and overheads of about 30% absorb most of the gross-margin gain. The earnings base is clean: there is no adjusted-earnings culture, and FY2025 reported EPS of 7.50 matched the brokers' 7.46. Financial leverage is low: net financial debt excluding leases is about EUR 1.0bn, and net debt including leases of EUR 4.3bn is about 1.2x trailing EBITDA (the 1.9x shown by FactSet is a data error, explained in the end notes); the credit ratings are S&P A and Moody's A3. Capital spending is about 2% of sales. The weakness is working capital, which rose to 22.5% of sales at the end of 2025 from 18.3% a year earlier (the third-quarter 25.1% is a seasonal peak), so 2025 free cash flow was negative on FactSet's definition.

Evidence on management. Gulden's record is the strongest part of the case. At Puma (2013 to 2022) sales rose 2.8 times and the operating margin rose from 2.1% to 7.6%. At adidas, every full year since 2023 has beaten the initial operating-profit guide by EUR 0.2bn to 0.9bn; the Yeezy stock was sold for EUR 1.4bn without material write-offs; inventory was cut 23% in 2023; and currency-neutral growth of 14% in the second quarter of 2026 came against a negative sector median. Gulden's ambition is high and growth-first (share gains every year, a USD 10bn North American run-rate, "about EUR 2bn of sales growth a year"), tempered by his aim to "avoid the boom-and-bust cycle". The culture is congruent with the strategy but depends on one personality.

Inference. adidas's foundation is adequate, not excellent. The foundation is good enough to sustain a 10% to 11% operating margin and high-single-digit growth while the brand is hot, but not good enough to make that path predictable or to close the returns gap with Nike. The industry structure gives adidas a deep profit pool and high barriers at the top, but not stable market shares or stable competitor behaviour, and 2027 is the high-water mark of external support.

So what. The model should hold a wider range on revenue than on gross margin, because brand heat moves volume faster than price. adidas should be valued as a good brand compounder in a cyclical, fashion-exposed industry, not as a quality compounder.

Counter-case. adidas is in its best relative position since about 2017, and its moats (running credibility, China localisation, athlete lock-ups) are widening. Asics, whose operating margin rose from 14.8% to 17.6% in 2025 on performance-led growth, shows that a performance engine can carry a brand to a higher margin than adidas targets. What would change my view: return on invested capital above 20% on the broad definition for two years; or a second lifestyle franchise emerging without a markdown cycle in the first.

Market view against mine. The market prices adidas below the general apparel retailers (Inditex 22.9x, Next 16.1x) and in line with the sports names at their multiple floors (JD Sports 6.4x, Zalando 10.3x), even though adidas has the highest consensus EPS growth in its peer table (+29%, +21% and +17% in FY2026 to FY2028). I think that discount reflects doubt about how long adidas's growth lasts and how cyclical the brand is, not doubt about its reinvestment runway. The doubt is partly right (about 2028) and partly wrong (about 2027).

#4 Guidance and delivery: a sandbagged profit floor beaten four years running, and a sales guide with no buffer

Conclusion: adidas's profit guidance is a sandbagged floor with a four-year record of being beaten, but its 2027 sales ambition carries no buffer, so the upside to guidance is in the margin and the risk is in the top line.

Score: 74, set by the Rater. Every full year since 2023 beat the initial operating-profit guide by EUR 0.2-0.9bn with raises in steps, nine beats and two in-line in twelve quarters before the self-inflicted, badly signalled Q2 2026 miss, and the profit guide ('about 10%' for 2027) is a moderately conservative floor. Held back because consensus already sits on guidance, the sales ambition carries no buffer and a new CFO's first guide is more likely cautious (group: guidance 70, sell-side 48); a record of skill rather than Maersk's freight luck, but current conservatism is weaker, so just below Maersk's 75 and above Odfjell's 70.

Evidence on the record. Under Gulden, adidas sets low initial profit guidance, raises it in steps and then delivers it precisely. FY2024's guide was raised three times; FY2025's initial guide of EUR 1.75bn sat well below the street's EUR 2.0bn before it was raised to EUR 2.0bn. FY2026's guide was raised in October from EUR 2.3bn to about EUR 2.5bn after the EUR 200m tariff refund and net of EUR 100m reinvested, so the underlying raise was only about EUR 0.1bn, the smallest relative upgrade of Gulden's tenure. Sales guidance for 2026 went from high single digits to 9% to 10% in July and was raised again in October.

The quarterly record is equally strong. adidas reported nine profit beats and two in-line results in the twelve quarters before the second-quarter 2026 miss; that miss (EBIT 7.9% below consensus on a 1.7% sales beat) came from management's own choice to spend. The third quarter of 2026 then beat again: EBIT of EUR 1,008m against consensus of EUR 742m, or about EUR 808m before the refund, about 9% above. Three practices make the guidance more reliable: contingent items such as the refund are excluded until received; the marketing ratio is guided, which is unusual and useful; and the mid-term targets are restated every quarter. Management's informal commentary runs above the formal guide on demand (China "on fire", all three running families strong for 2027, Europe back to high-single-digit growth in the fourth quarter, "confidence in 2027 increasing") and at or below the formal guide on profit conversion.

Evidence on consensus. Consensus now sits on guidance for both years. FY2026 consensus EBIT is EUR 2,517m against guidance of "about EUR 2.5bn"; FY2027 consensus EBIT is EUR 2,894m, exactly the 10% margin target applied to consensus revenue. Before the second-quarter miss, consensus sat above guidance (EUR 2.5bn against EUR 2.3bn); the miss anchored analysts to the targets. The visible FY2027 EPS range runs from EUR 9.84 (AlphaValue) to 12.57 (StoneX), and the five houses that shape the narrative (Bernstein, Deutsche Bank, Redburn, Jefferies, Morgan Stanley) average about 11.9, 3% above the FactSet median.

Inference. adidas's profit guidance is a reliable floor, not a forecast; its current sales guidance, unusually, is not low. The years 2024 to 2026 rode a recovery from a trough, Nike's weakness, clean channels and the World Cup; 2027 keeps only part of the first and loses the last two. Adjusted for those change forces, the sales target of "high single digits" is neutral to slightly ambitious, while the margin target of "about 10%" is moderately conservative. The margin levers (the hedges, a contracted marketing load falling from EUR 1.58bn in 2026 to about EUR 1.1bn a year, and sourcing) point to a 10.3% to 10.5% margin before reinvestment, and Bernstein and Redburn both model 10.5%. The new CFO's first guide on 10 March 2027 is more likely to be cautious than generous, with the probabilities shown below.

So what. Three practical readings follow. Treat the FY2026 outcome as a small beat that is mostly spent: the fourth quarter needs about EUR 240m of EBIT after the EUR 100m charge, against about EUR 165m to 180m a year earlier, which the catch-up of ERP-delayed shipments makes likely. Treat the 2027 margin as delivered rather than exceeded. Treat the sales guide as the half most likely to be trimmed.

Counter-case. adidas's management team has not yet been tested by a year of low organic growth. Its only miss in three years came from its own spending choice and was punished severely. Its habit of reinvesting windfalls also means that a 10% margin can be delivered while the underlying business is weaker than the reported figure suggests. What would change my view: a March guide that replaces "high single digits" with "mid single digits" and also trims the margin; or a first-quarter 2027 gross margin that fails to show the hedge benefit.

Market view against mine. Street consensus sits on the guide. I expect the profit guide to be met with a small, mostly reinvested beat, which is in line with the street's EPS and about 3% below the quality houses. I differ in expecting the sales guide to be trimmed first and the profit guide to be raised later, so that the revision pattern inside 2027 changes the composition of earnings rather than their level.

#5 Operating leverage and pricing power: EPS grows about 2.5 times as fast as revenue, but management caps the flow-through

Conclusion: adidas's business model turns revenue growth into profit growth at about two to three times after management's reinvestment and about four times before it, and buybacks add three points of EPS growth a year. EPS therefore compounds at mid-teens rates on mid-single-digit revenue growth, but management's reinvestment caps the upside, and adidas's pricing power rests on brand heat, not structure.

Score: 67, set by the Rater. Structurally strong operating leverage: contribution after variable costs is about 42% of sales against fixed and contracted costs of 32-33%, so 1% of revenue moves EBIT about 4%, proven both ways (FY2024 EBIT five-fold on +10.5% sales; marketing cut 23% in 2020), plus buybacks adding about 3 points of EPS a year and EUR 300-400m of gross cost-out; EPS 14-16% on 5.5-6% revenue is about 2.5 times, above the Universe's 2 times. Held below 75 because management caps flow-through by reinvesting (realised 2-3 times), pricing power is mix and markdown discipline in a fashion brand rather than structural, and financial gearing adds little; coherent with Economic strength 60 and Financial forecasts 68.

Evidence on the cost structure. adidas's contribution after variable costs (about 42% of sales) far exceeds its fixed and contracted costs (about 32% to 33%), which is the source of its operating leverage. The cost lines are:

  • Cost of goods, about 48% of sales, all variable.
  • Marketing and point-of-sale, about 12% of sales (about EUR 3.25bn). About half was contracted in 2026, but only about a third will be contracted from 2027; campaign spend can be flexed within a quarter, and the marketing ratio fell to 11.5% in the third quarter from 13.7% in the second.
  • Operating overheads, about 31% of sales for the full year (29.7% in the first nine months). About a third varies with sales (direct-channel freight, warehouse and store labour, platform fees), and two-thirds is fixed. Depreciation of about EUR 1.2bn, including right-of-use assets, sits inside overheads; lease payments of about EUR 0.75bn a year sit outside EBITDA.

Evidence on how management uses the leverage. Realised leverage is lower than the structural 4 times and asymmetric, because management decides how much of each revenue gain reaches profit. FY2024 revenue growth of 10.5% lifted operating profit five-fold through gross margin, and FY2025's incremental margin was 64%. But second-quarter 2026 sales growth of 14% currency-neutral produced EBIT growth of only 5%, because management chose to spend, and the EUR 200m tariff refund became a EUR 0.2bn guidance raise only after EUR 100m was reinvested. In our base case the incremental EBIT margin is about 31% in 2027 (on the clean 2026 base) and 13% to 19% thereafter. On the downside, marketing is the shock absorber (cut 23% in 2020 and 8% in 2023) while overheads are sticky (−5% in 2020, +1% in 2023), so a revenue shortfall costs up to twice what an equal revenue beat adds.

Evidence on pricing power. adidas's realised prices are rising in real terms through mix and fewer markdowns, not through list prices. Average selling prices rose about 3% in the third quarter on a mix shift toward premium collections, and realised prices rose by double digits in the US and the major Western markets in mid-2026. adidas's own direct-channel markdown breadth is stable at 29%, against 42% for Nike, 47% for Jordan and 74% for Nike's Dunk at DICK'S. The Adizero running line sells primarily at full price, and the running price ladder runs from EUR 500 down to EUR 150. The erosion is in lifestyle: nearly half of Gazelle styles are discounted on adidas's own site, an online retailer saw markdown penetration rise eight to nine points in September, and an online buyer in the German-speaking (DACH) markets reports lifestyle footwear sales down 25% to 30%. Management is also withdrawing the concessions it gave retailers in 2023 to 2025, which tightens wholesale terms in adidas's favour. From here, price and mix add about 1.5 to 2.5 points of revenue growth a year but are roughly neutral to gross margin, because cheaper running iterations (Hyperboost at EUR 120 to 130 in 2027 against EUR 200 at launch) and "more commercial price points" in Europe offset the premium mix.

Evidence on financial leverage and buybacks. Debt barely amplifies EPS, but buybacks do. Net interest is about EUR 215m in 2026 and falls to EUR 175m by 2030, and a 100 basis point move in rates changes EPS by only 0.5% to 2% because the debt is largely fixed-rate. A EUR 1bn buyback each year at about 13x earnings (an earnings yield near 7.7% against an after-tax cost of cash of about 2.5%) cuts the average share count by about 3% a year, from 175.3m in 2026 to 155.6m in 2030, and adds about 2% to EPS per EUR 1bn, net of forgone interest. The balance sheet also holds an unused option, outside the base case, of EUR 3bn to 4bn of further buyback capacity under the 2.0x leverage ceiling.

Evidence on cost-out. About EUR 300m to 400m of gross annual efficiencies (100 to 140 basis points of sales) is available by 2028, but only about half is likely to reach EBIT. The sources are marketing normalisation in non-tournament years (50 to 100 basis points); sourcing (about 100 basis points gross, capped near 70 net by supplier distress, with Yue Yuen's nine-month profit down 50% to 55%, Huali's margins at record lows and Lai Yih 58.6% dependent on adidas); and overhead simplification (50 to 100 basis points over three years, as the SAP S/4HANA migration completes). Only about half reaches EBIT because management reinvests, and because the tournament calendar (the Women's World Cup in 2027, the European Championship in 2028 and the World Cup in 2030) keeps marketing near 12% of sales.

Feedback loops. adidas's reinforcing loops act mostly on margin, and its balancing loops act mostly on revenue. Through the first half of 2027 the reinforcing loops dominate gross margin while the World Cup base effect dominates revenue; from the second half of 2027, the balancing loops dominate both. Direct-to-consumer sales are already 43% of the total, against the 40% structural target, so further channel mix gives little more margin.

Inference and so what. Revenue growth produces outsized profit growth only within a band that management sets. EPS can grow 14% to 16% a year on revenue growth of 5.5% to 6% because gross margin, the cost ratios and the share count each add a few points. EPS will not grow 30% on 10% revenue growth, however, because management will spend the surplus. The model should therefore carry wide revenue ranges and narrow margin ranges, and the asymmetry (a downside wider than the upside) belongs in the risk analysis, not in the base case.

To judge adidas's momentum, read gross margin and the cost ratios, not the EBIT line.Management steers the margin to its target and reinvests windfalls, so EPS beats will be small and frequent.

Counter-case. The "cost of brand heat" may have risen structurally, which was Jefferies' worry after the second quarter; Nike's demand-creation spending is 11.2% of revenue and rising. If so, the 10% margin slips and the cost-out never reaches EBIT. If the terrace decline turns into clearance through wholesale, 50 to 100 basis points of gross margin go with it. What would change my view: lifestyle markdown breadth above about 40% at the large US and European retailers; or a 2027 marketing guide above 12% of sales.

Market view against mine. The street sees "limited flow-through" (Morgan Stanley) and resents the reinvestment habit. I see the same habit as the reason the margin is predictable, and I would rather the market read gross margin than EBIT. Nobody models the fall in the contracted marketing load, which gives management about a point of sales of protection in a bad year.

#6 Forecasts: EPS compounds at 14% to 16% a year to 2030 on revenue growth of 5.5% to 6%

Conclusion: our forecasts describe a company moving from recovery to compounding. EPS grows 14% to 16% a year to 2030 on revenue growth of 5.5% to 6%, because gross margin, the cost ratios and buybacks each add a few points. 2027 EBIT and EPS are relatively predictable; revenue, and footwear especially, is the line to widen; and 2028 is the year to doubt.

Score: 90, set by the Rater. The clean base is the honest one because the EUR 200m tariff refund is a one-off, which puts the measure just inside A's 15-30% band. Placed at the floor because growth is front-loaded (+25% in 2027, then +16%, +12%, +12%), about 3 points a year come from buybacks, organic revenue is only 5.5-6%, and the margin returns to its 2019 peak (10.5-10.8%) rather than exceeding it.

The forecasts. Our forecasts sit within 1% of consensus on 2027 EBIT and EPS but below consensus on revenue. The EPS line below is the Analyst's cross-check, which corrects two data artefacts in the model's own EPS line (see the end notes).

The 2027 EBIT bridge. 2027 EBIT rises about EUR 440m, from a clean 2026 base of about EUR 2,428m (an 8.9% margin) to about EUR 2,867m (10.0%), and about 60% of the rise is locked or semi-locked. Gross margin contributes the largest step (+60 basis points net, about EUR 170m); volume at the prior margin contributes about EUR 130m (+5.5% on EUR 27.1bn); overhead leverage contributes about EUR 85m (+30 basis points, as overheads grow 4% in euros against revenue growth of 5.5%); and marketing's return to 11.8% of sales contributes about EUR 55m. The dollar hedge alone (about EUR 230m) is larger than the whole volume contribution and is the most locked of the drivers. The demand-dependent share of the bridge, meaning volume plus the market-driven offsets inside gross margin, is about 40%.

From EBIT to EPS. The step from EBIT to EPS is now almost mechanical. Net financial items are about EUR 195m in 2027 (largely fixed-rate debt plus lease interest of about EUR 100m), the all-in charge for tax and minorities is 26.5% of pre-tax profit, and the share count falls about 3% a year. Of the 25% rise in EPS from the clean FY2026 figure of 9.24 to 11.57 in FY2027, EBIT growth contributes about 20 points, the lower financial charge about one point and the smaller share count three to three and a half points.

The revenue composition. 2027 revenue growth of 5.5% depends on footwear (+7.5% from a base of about EUR 14.4bn) offsetting a nearly flat apparel line (+1.5% from about EUR 10.7bn). Inside footwear, running (about EUR 2.3bn) grows 20% to 25%, the terrace franchises (about EUR 1.5bn to 2bn) fall 12% to 15%, the Superstar and Stan Smith relaunches add volume, and adidas gains Chinese shelf space from January. Inside apparel, national-team product falls by about EUR 0.8bn to 0.9bn while the rest grows about 10%. Accessories grow about 4%.

The quarterly shape of 2027 matters for how the year will be read. Revenue growth runs at about +4%, +2.5%, +7% and +8.5% through the four quarters, with the second quarter the low point. Reported third-quarter 2027 EBIT will fall year on year (about EUR 985m against EUR 1,008m) because the 2026 refund sits in the comparison base, even though the underlying margin rises about 150 basis points. Fourth-quarter EBIT then rises sharply as it laps the EUR 100m charge.

Cash. Free cash flow after leases and all capital spending is about EUR 1.7bn in 2027 and EUR 1.9bn in 2028, or 0.85 to 0.88 times net income. The calculation starts from brokers' EBITDA and deducts cash tax, non-lease interest, working capital (the ratio eases from 22.5% to 21.5% of sales by 2028), capital spending (rising from EUR 520m to 740m) and lease principal of about EUR 700m; lease interest sits within financial items. Free cash flow covers the dividend (EUR 0.75bn to 1.0bn) and EUR 1bn of buybacks; net debt including leases stays near EUR 4bn, and leverage falls from about 1.1x to 0.8x EBITDA as EBITDA grows. FY2026 cash depends on the usual fourth-quarter working-capital release of about EUR 0.6bn, and a year-end operating working-capital ratio above 24% of sales would be the warning sign.

Scope for double-digit growth and for more than the past. The forecast years are a slower, steadier and higher-quality version of FY2019 to FY2025, when revenue grew only 0.8% a year, net income ranged from EUR −119m to 1,917m and free cash flow from EUR −1,774m to 2,206m. In the forecasts, revenue grows about 6% a year; the operating margin recovers to the 2019 peak (10.5% to 10.8%) but not beyond it; EPS compounds at about 14% a year from the reported 2026 base and 16% from the clean base; and cash is positive every year and returned to shareholders. Double-digit EPS growth is well supported through 2028. Beyond 2028, EPS growth settles at about 10% to 12% a year: high-single-digit revenue growth plus three points from the buyback. Margins above the past are not in the forecast, because a margin above 12% would need Nike-like scale and returns.

Where our forecasts differ, and why. Our forecasts sit below consensus mainly on revenue, because of the World Cup comparison and footwear, and below management mainly on growth and overheads.

The FY2027 range of outcomes. Our range for FY2027 is EBIT of EUR 2.55bn to 3.1bn (a 9.0% to 10.6% margin) and EPS of 10.2 to 12.6 around a base of 11.6. Weighting the cases (25% bear at 10.2 to 10.6, 55% base, 20% bull at 12.3 to 12.6) gives a probability-weighted EPS of about 11.5, close to the base, which is the test that the base case is not optimistic. The sell-side's range for FY2027 EPS coincides almost exactly with ours. For 2028 the range of outcomes roughly doubles.

I change no forecast input. The model's latest update raised 2027 revenue growth by half a point, to 5.5%, on supplier order data, which is the right lean, and every margin, cash and balance-sheet input matches my own judgements in #1 to #5.

#7 Scope for upgrades over 6 to 12 months: small and back-loaded, with revenue trimmed before profit is raised

Conclusion: the scope for upgrades is real but small and back-loaded: the sales line is trimmed first and the profit line raised later. The favourable surprise over 6 to 12 months is therefore the predictability of adidas's 2027 earnings, not their level.

Score: 52, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is more likely met than raised in March 2027 (50% in line, 30% a sales-only trim, 10% a cut on both), with a profit raise of EUR 0.1-0.15bn (about 4% of EBIT, roughly 0.6 of the 6% revenue growth rate) at about 55% odds in July or October and a cut at about 20%. FY2027 consensus EPS is expected to be held (40% within 3%, 30% up, 30% down) with revenue trimmed 1-3%, and the narrative gap (a locked margin bridge) is modest, so the expected net change is close to zero (about the 40th percentile) with mildly positive guidance odds, coherent with the group's 54; just below Spie's 54 and above Kerry's 49.

Evidence on guidance. The machinery for upgrades is in place, but it must work through a sales trim first. adidas's record says a profit raise is about three times as likely as a profit cut. The structure of the 2027 bridge says that a raise, if it comes, will be a gross-margin event. The calendar says that it will come in July or October 2027, after the World Cup comparison has been absorbed. Any raise is likely to be EUR 0.1bn to 0.15bn, with the rest of the surplus spent. The calendar below sets out each event.

Evidence on consensus. FY2027 consensus EPS (median 11.64) is more likely to be held than moved: within 3% either way in twelve months (40%), more than 3% higher (30%) or more than 3% lower (30%). Revenue consensus is likely to be cut by 1% to 3% in the first half of 2027, while consensus EBIT and EPS are held or edged up by 1% to 3% from the second half as the hedge benefit appears in reported margins. The arithmetic explains why: consensus EBIT already embeds a 10% margin on 7.5% growth, and our 10% margin on 5.5% growth reduces consensus EBIT by only about EUR 25m, which is inside the noise of a single quarter. Three low outliers (AlphaValue 9.84, UBS 10.77, Santander 11.10) also pull down the FactSet median, so if the quality houses hold their estimates, the median can rise as the outliers drop out. FY2028 consensus EPS (13.64) is more likely to be cut by 3% to 5% in March 2028, to about 13.0 to 13.2, near our corrected 13.4, when the 2028 hedge rates and a reframed ambition for growth and overheads are absorbed.

Evidence on the narrative. The sell-side describes every dynamic in the case but has not combined their arithmetic. The gap between what is known and what is connected is favourable for 2027 and unfavourable for 2028 (Morgan Stanley's own gap table calls 2028 "completely unmapped"). The proxies for investor positioning describe holders who own the stock on valuation, are braced for the lifestyle rollover and are waiting for a reason to add: options priced the bear case at over three times the bull case in August; short interest is under 2%; 63% of analysts rate the stock a buy; the shares fell 12% on a cost miss and rose 5.8% on the third-quarter beat; and Deutsche Bank describes "no catalyst narrative disguising strong operational delivery". Direct investor commentary in the research is thin.

Inference. The narrative most likely to change is from "a lifestyle brand past its peak" to "a performance-led compounder with rising margins and buybacks". The April and July 2027 results are where that new narrative is tested, because they will show gross margin rising while apparel laps the tournament. The two catalysts the sell-side highlights (the Nike investor day and the March guide) are both framed as risks, so a non-event at either is a positive surprise.

So what. Upgrades over 6 to 12 months are modest in size and favourable in shape: one profit raise to guidance, consensus EPS held while revenue estimates are cut, and revision breadth turning mildly negative around March and April and mildly positive after July. The case does not rest on the market being wrong about the level of 2027 earnings; it rests on the market being wrong about how predictable those earnings are.

Counter-case. A Nike plan that retailers judge credible for spring 2027 would raise the probability of a sales trim in March and a profit cut in April or July, and would pull the quality houses toward the low UBS estimate; a weak European holiday season would do the same. What would change my view: FY2027 consensus EPS below 11.0 by May 2027; or the Master Dashboard's revision-momentum letter back at F.

Market view against mine. Consensus expects revenue growth of 7.5% and a 10% margin in 2027; I expect 5.5% growth and a 10% margin. I expect the street to end 2027 at about 6% to 6.5% growth with the margin at or slightly above 10%, so that the narrative registers revenue cuts and profit holding in the same year.

#8 Current momentum: estimates have stopped falling, but the share price has not yet confirmed the turn

Conclusion: momentum has turned from falling to flat on estimates and from F to C on the Master Dashboard's letters, but price momentum is not yet confirmed and the sector's largest dated event is twelve days away. adidas is at the start of a momentum turn, not in one.

Score: 77, set by the Rater. Both measures are above 50 and no part is strongly negative, so B: guidance was raised in October, the buy share is up 5 points to 63%, the sell-side letter moved from F to C and the narrative turned after Q3. Placed low in the band because three-month EPS revisions are -1% (35th percentile) and flat at six months, the 200-day average is flat with the 50-day below the 150-day, and the sports peers are weak (peers do not lower the letter).

Evidence on guidance and estimates. Guidance momentum is positive and recent. FY2026 profit guidance was raised on 20 October 2026 in an ad hoc pre-announcement, sales guidance was raised twice during the year, and the mid-term targets have been reaffirmed every quarter. Estimate momentum has stopped falling and is now flat. After twelve-month cuts to consensus EPS of 12.6% (FY2026), 10.8% (FY2027) and 8.9% (FY2028), the six-month changes are +0.3%, −0.1% and −1.7%, and the one-month changes are +2.2%, −0.3% and −1.7%. The share of analysts rating the stock a buy is 63%, up 5 points in six months. The Master Dashboard's revision-momentum score is 9, and its sell-side momentum letter is C, up from F in August.

The mean target price is EUR 201.87 and the median EUR 200, 16% above the share price, within a range from EUR 156 (UBS, rated Sell after a downgrade on 3 November) to EUR 250 (Metzler). Narrative momentum turned with the third-quarter results (Jefferies: scepticism "has started to dissipate"; Deutsche Bank: "confidence in 2027 increasing"), with the Nike investor day as the overhang.

Evidence on the share price. Price momentum is only letter C, because the long-term trend has not yet turned. The price is 12.3% above a 200-day average of EUR 153.96, but that average has risen in only one of the last twelve months, and the 50-day average (EUR 150.59) is below the 150-day average (EUR 157.37). Relative strength is at the 65th percentile of the universe. The stock has rallied about 19% from its end-September close of EUR 145 on the pre-announced beat, within a 52-week range of EUR 127.56 to 188.80. Valuation is letter A, at the 1st percentile of the stock's ten-year P/E range, while the dashboard's thematic-momentum letter for the sector is F. Over a rolling six months, the apparel-retail basket explains about a third of the daily variance in adidas's shares (correlation 0.56, beta 0.94) and two-thirds is the stock's own; the sports subset (Puma, Zalando, JD Sports) explains more than the rest of the basket combined.

+6.0%three-month return
+17.7%six-month return
+16.0%nine-month return
+8.6%twelve-month return

Evidence on peers. The sports names (adidas, JD Sports, Zalando, Nike) sit at their multiple floors with weak earnings momentum, while the general apparel retailers sit near their peaks. Puma's 28.6x is a multiple of depressed earnings, and its +54.6% over twelve months comes from a low base after a 24% inventory reduction. JD Sports has cut its profit guide and reports flat spring 2027 pre-orders for Nike product. Nike's shares fell 52.6% in the twelve months to October 2026, Nike has paused buybacks, and its investor day on 16 and 17 November is the sector's next dated event. On's and Hoka's growth is slowing.

Inference. adidas has the best earnings momentum of the sports names and the lowest multiple percentile in the whole peer table. Its momentum is "stabilised and turning", not "strong". A technical letter of C with a flat 200-day average means the share price has not yet confirmed what the third-quarter results said; a 200-day average rising for three consecutive months would be the confirmation.

So what. adidas is not a momentum entry. It is a valuation-and-delivery entry, with momentum that could become supportive from the July 2027 results. The next twelve days carry the largest sentiment event (Nike's investor day), and adidas's share price reacts severely to news, mostly for company-specific reasons.

Counter-case. Momentum measures lag: the dashboard letters were F three months ago, and the stock has already rallied 19%. A strong Nike plan would send the sector's letters back down together. What would change my view: the 200-day average rising for three months and sales revisions positive for two quarters (momentum confirmed); or EPS revisions negative for two consecutive months after March 2027 (momentum broken).

Market view against mine. The market reads the third quarter as a one-off beat flattered by the tariff refund. I read the underlying 9% beat, the inventory discipline and the supplier order data as the start of a stabilisation, and I read the flat 200-day average as a lag rather than a verdict.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity: a predictable number made in an unpredictable way

Conclusion: 2027 earnings are a reasonably predictable number (within about 10% either way, skewed down in profit and balanced in revenue) made in a reasonably unpredictable way. The riskiness of the case sits in the second half of the 18 months, in the multiple and in the share price's severe reaction to misses, not in the base-case arithmetic.

Score: 56, set by the Rater. The FY2027 EPS cone is 10.2-12.6 around 11.6 (about -12%/+9%) with about 60% of the EBIT bridge locked by hedges, contracts and buybacks, low fixed-rate leverage (net debt/EBITDA 1.3x, A rated), four trackable drivers and supplier data that lead by a quarter or two. Against that, a single-brand fashion business whose revenue turns on footwear finding a terrace successor, a cone that doubles in 2028, a 12%-in-a-day reaction function, and correlated sudden risks (tariffs on Vietnam, South-East Asian supply, China nationalism); between the group's 47 and 60, so just above NKT's 54 and below Banca Generali's 60.

Simplicity. The case reduces to two lines moving in opposite directions with different predictability. The margin line is locked by hedges, contracts and a management that steers to its target. The revenue line depends on footwear finding a successor to the terrace franchises while adidas laps the World Cup and Nike's absence. Below EBIT the business is clean and mechanical. The drivers are concentrated rather than diffuse: four drivers make the 2027 EBIT bridge, one swing factor (footwear) makes the revenue risk, and three dated items (the hedge roll, Nike's new ranges and the second year of terrace decline) make the 2028 risk. That makes the case simpler than most consumer-brand cases. There are two complications. Because the margin is managed, the EBIT figure is less informative than gross margin and the cost ratios. And the share price reacts severely: it fell 12% in a day on an 8% EBIT miss that came with a sales beat, and it rose 5.8% on the pre-announced beat.

Five judgements move the shares most: four for 2027 and one for 2028. Each is sized below for a plausible error. All are on the FY2027 base of revenue EUR 28.6bn, EBIT EUR 2,867m, EPS 11.57, 169.7m shares and a 26.5% all-in tax rate (so EUR 100m of EBIT is about EUR 0.43 of EPS), and a 13x two-year-forward multiple (so EUR 1 of EPS is about EUR 13 of share price, or 7.5% of the price).

  1. Footwear growth in 2027 (base +7.5%). If footwear grows 2.5% instead, revenue falls short by about EUR 720m (2.5% of the group). At a 42% contribution margin, the shortfall costs about EUR 300m of EBIT before management acts (−10.5%). If management cuts campaign marketing by half a point of sales (about EUR 145m), the net EBIT shortfall is about EUR 155m (−5.4%). EPS falls to about 10.3 unmitigated or 10.9 mitigated, and at an unchanged 13x the shares are worth EUR 9 to 17 less, or 5% to 10%. In the other direction, footwear growth of 12.5% (roughly the path consensus implies) adds EUR 720m of revenue and about EUR 300m of EBIT before reinvestment, of which perhaps half reaches EPS: about +0.65, to 12.2.
  2. The 2027 gross margin (base 52.4%: +60 basis points net, of which the hedge is +80). Each 10 basis points of gross margin is EUR 29m of EBIT and EUR 0.12 of EPS. If promotions from Nike's clearance and the liquidation of Chinese inventory absorb the hedge gain and the margin lands at 51.9% (the bear case), EBIT is about EUR 145m lower (−5%) and EPS about 10.95. If the hedge delivers Bernstein's +115 basis points and the margin reaches 52.8%, EBIT is about EUR 115m higher before reinvestment, and EPS is about 0.25 higher, at about 11.8, after half is spent.
  3. The marketing and overhead ratios management chooses (base marketing 11.8% of sales, overheads 30.8%). Each half-point of sales on either line is about EUR 143m of EBIT and EUR 0.62 of EPS (5.4%). If a Nike marketing push forces adidas to hold marketing at 12.3% in 2027, EPS is about 10.95; if a cost programme brings overheads to 30.3% a year early, EPS is about 12.2. This judgement is the one most in management's hands, and it is the one that caps the upside.
  4. The multiple, which depends on whether the concern about Nike passes (base: today's 13x on two-year-forward EPS of about 13.1, rising to about 15.5 by March 2028). Each turn of the multiple on the March 2028 EPS base is worth about EUR 15.5 a share, or 9% of today's price. A move from 13x to the ten-year 10th percentile (16.3x) is worth about EUR 51 a share (+30%); to the 35th percentile (19.7x), about EUR 104 (+61%); and to the five-year low (11x), about −EUR 31 (−18%). No earnings judgement in this list moves the shares as much as the multiple does, which is why the lifecycle (#10) and the fair multiple (#11) matter more than the EPS range.
  5. For 2028, the roll of the dollar hedges (base −20 to −40 basis points of gross margin, offset by sourcing and mix). If the euro falls to about 1.05 dollars and the 2028 hedges roll 100 basis points worse than 2027's, 2028 EBIT falls about EUR 300m (−9.5%) and EPS about 1.35, to about 12.1. Each 1% change in the realised dollar cost is worth about EUR 70m to 75m of EBIT before mitigation. Currency also cuts across years: a stronger dollar lifts 2027 reported revenue through translation while hurting 2028, so currency narrows the 2027 EPS range and widens 2028's.

Fragilities and requirements. The base case requires four things. Footwear growth must re-accelerate from about +1% to +7.5%, which is at the edge of what adidas has demonstrated: the Superstar and Stan Smith rollover of 2017 to 2019 cost about EUR 500m of sales in one year, and footwear grew only 3% to 5% for several quarters. Apparel outside football must grow about 10% while jersey sales fall. The spring 2027 order book, which management can see and the market cannot, must be as resilient as supplier data suggest (Huali; Lai Yih +14% in September; Pou Chen +10.4%; Yue Yuen +6.6%). And the hedge must land as modelled. The base case does not require the 2028 ambitions to be met, a cost programme, a working-capital release or a mania multiple.

Sudden, high-magnitude risks. Ranked by plausibility times impact over 18 months, the sudden risks are mostly low in plausibility, but several are correlated through South-East Asia and the dollar.

Trackability. The case is easy to track on ratios and hard to track on the football and franchise mix. Every quarter adidas reports currency-neutral growth by region, channel and category, the marketing and overhead ratios, inventory ageing and a qualitative gross-margin bridge; it reports the hedge book once a year, and the 2028 rates arrive with the annual report in early March 2027. adidas does not disclose football, terrace or running revenue, or its order books. Those come from Bernstein's franchise-level markdown trackers, Masterlink's shipment forecasts for Lai Yih, the monthly sales of Topsports and Pou Sheng, and the suppliers' monthly sales on the tenth of each month, which led adidas's wholesale turning points by three to six months in 2018 to 2019 and in 2023. A turn toward the bear case would therefore be visible within a quarter of its start. The milestones to watch are ratios, as the table shows.

Sector precedents and cyclicality. In sportswear, outperformance has come from brand heat plus a product cycle plus margin recovery (adidas 2015 to 2018; Puma 2013 to 2022; adidas 2023 to 2026). Underperformance has come from a lifestyle franchise peaking into a glut (adidas 2017 to 2018; Nike 2022 to 2026, whose three big franchises peaked at about 30% of revenue, against 8% to 15% for adidas's terrace franchises, and cost a 300 to 350 basis point gross-margin drag) or from a geographic shock (adidas in China in 2021; the Yeezy termination in 2022, when EBIT fell from EUR 1,963m to 573m). The two live precedents for 2027 point in opposite directions. Lululemon's gross margin fell 230 basis points on fixed-cost deleverage as growth slowed, which is the shape of the bear case; Asics's margin rose 280 basis points on performance-led growth, which is the shape of the bull case. adidas has Asics's levers and Lululemon's franchise exposure. The sector rule that shares are punished for cost-led misses, even when sales beat, applies to adidas with full force. Cyclicality is moderate: adidas's revenue has been through a pandemic, a boycott and a franchise termination in six years, and consumer discretionary is the current market regime's most disliked sector.

Market view against mine. The market prices the case as if 2027 EPS depended on the lifestyle cycle; I think about 60% of the 2027 EBIT bridge is independent of it. The market also treats the Nike investor day as the main fundamental risk. I treat the investor day as the main sentiment risk, and I date the fundamental Nike risk to Nike's autumn 2027 range and its fiscal 2028.

#10 Lifecycle: turning up, with delivery ahead of the narrative and the multiple

Conclusion: adidas is turning up. Its fundamental delivery is already in the reinforcing phase, but the narrative and the multiple are two to four quarters behind, so the Master Dashboard's "Reinforcing" label is premature as a description of the stock, even if it is fair as a description of the company.

Score: 63, set by the Rater. The memo's 'turning up' is right and the computed Reinforcing premature: delivery is reinforcing, the multiple has stopped falling from 28x to 13x and the price is 12% above a 200-day average that has only just stopped falling, but revisions are flat, momentum letters are C and the thesis is not broadening. Growth itself decelerates (revenue to 5.5%, EPS +25% then 12-16%) with 2028 the year to doubt, so it is a valuation-led turn more than accelerating fundamentals; below Kerry's mid-cycle 67 and above Nexans' paused 61.

Evidence. The Master Dashboard's rule classifies adidas as "Reinforcing" and assigns that phase's guideline multiple, the 90th percentile of 28.03x. Read phase by phase, the fundamentals tell a different story:

  • Delivery is reinforcing: four years of initial guidance beaten, nine beats in twelve quarters and a record third quarter.
  • The thesis is not yet broadening: the narrative is still "peak terrace", revisions are flat, the FY2027 revenue line is being argued down rather than up, and no house models the cost programme or the locked bridge.
  • The price and the multiple have bottomed and are turning up: the two-year-forward P/E fell from 28x in May 2024 to 11.1x in September 2026; the shares hit a 52-week low of EUR 127.56 in the spring and have rallied 19% since September on the beat; the 200-day average has only just stopped falling; and the momentum letters are C.

The multiple is at the 1st percentile of its ten-year range but the 33rd percentile of its two-year range, because the stock has traded in a 12x to 16x band for most of the last eighteen months. The de-rating is complete; the re-rating has not begun.

Inference. The honest placement is "turning up", with delivery already reinforcing and the narrative and the multiple lagging by two to four quarters. That lag is both the opportunity and the risk. The stock moves to "thesis broadening" when the April and July 2027 results show gross margin rising, footwear growth back above 5% and a profit raise, and when Nike's spring range is in the shops without taking adidas's space. The multiple moves to "reinforcing" only when the sportswear group leaves the discount-cycle penalty box, which #1 dates to spring 2027 in North America. The stock falls back to "stalling" if lifestyle markdowns turn into clearance through wholesale, or if the March guide trims both sales and margin.

So what. The phase placement sets the fair multiple (#11) and the shape of the return (#12). A turning-up stock earns a multiple lower in its range than a reinforcing one, and most of the return comes from the first leg of the re-rating (from 13x to 16x and then 20x), not from the mania band.

Counter-case. The dashboard's rule may be right and my placement too cautious. On delivery alone adidas is already reinforcing, the sell-side momentum letter has moved up two notches in three months, and a stock whose EPS compounds at 14% to 16% with a buyback can broaden its thesis faster than the quarters suggest once the Nike overhang passes. What would change my view: two consecutive quarters of positive sales revisions with the 200-day average rising (then "thesis broadening"); or a profit cut in the first half of 2027 (then "stalling").

Market view against mine. The market's framing ("no catalyst", "peak terrace", "all eyes on Beaverton", meaning on Nike's headquarters) is a bottoming framing. I think the third-quarter results and the supplier data moved the stock to turning up, and that the market will not concede "thesis broadening" until the July 2027 results.

#11 The fair multiple: 19.7x, the ten-year 35th percentile, with 16.3x as the first stop

Conclusion: the fair multiple for a stock turning up from a sportswear-group de-rating is the ten-year 35th percentile of 19.7x on an 18-month view, with 16.3x as the first stop. The guideline's 28x is neither needed nor supported, because near-zero rates and trough earnings, not delivery, set that band.

Score: 92, set by the Rater. Cheap on both measures gives A, and both readings are deep (about 13x against a ten-year 10th percentile of 16.3x). Placed a little above the floor because part of the cheapness is deserved: the ten-year range was inflated by zero rates and trough-earnings multiples, growth is decelerating to mid-single digits and the stock sits only at the 33rd percentile of its two-year range, but a recovering margin, mid-teens EPS and buybacks still warrant more than 13x.

Evidence. Today's multiple of about 13x sits below every band of the ten-year range. The ten-year bands for the two-year-forward P/E (excluding outlier months far above normal) are: 10th percentile 16.3x ("crash"), 35th 19.7x ("conservative"), median 21.4x ("prudent"), 75th 24.7x ("defendable") and 90th 28.0x ("mania"). The five-year range is 10.9x to 34.5x with a median of 18.9x, and the two-year median is 13.9x. Today's reading is about 12.9x on the model's price and consensus two-year-forward EPS of 13.12 (13.2x on the dashboard's price). Viewforth's guideline sets the fair multiple from the lifecycle phase and the range: higher in the range for phases of peak delivery, lower for stalling or turning-up phases, where forecasts are more uncertain. The dashboard's rule gives "Reinforcing" and 28.03x, 153% above today's multiple.

Two features of the history matter for reading the bands. First, the ten-year 90th percentile was set in two periods that do not describe a reinforcing adidas: 2020 to 2021 (24x to 28x, when rates were near zero and the market paid for every consumer compounder) and 2023 to 2024 (27x to 32x, when the Yeezy termination and the inventory clean-up depressed forward earnings, so a trough-earnings denominator inflated the multiple). The top band is therefore partly an artefact of trough earnings, not a record of what the market paid for delivery. Second, the last time adidas delivered a 10% to 11% margin with high-single-digit growth and no reset (2018 to 2019), it traded at 17x to 24x; the last time it grew 12% to 13% currency-neutral with the recovery intact (late 2024 to early 2025), it traded at 20x to 22x.

Relative to peers, the low level of the multiple is a sportswear phenomenon: JD Sports sits at its 10th percentile, Zalando at its 5th and Frasers at its 21st, while Inditex, Next, OVS and H&M sit at their 83rd to 90th. A re-rating to the median therefore needs the sportswear group to re-rate as well as adidas.

My view. Because the phase is turning up (#10), the guideline points lower in the range. I set the fair multiple at 19.7x, the 35th percentile, on an 18-month view, conditional on the April and July 2027 results showing the hedge in gross margin and footwear back in growth. I treat 16.3x, the 10th percentile, as the first stop that the case must at least reach to work: it is the multiple of a stock whose compounding the market accepts but whose cyclicality it still prices. I do not use 28x, for three reasons: nothing in the fundamentals or the history supports the mania band for a company whose margin target is a return to its old peak; adidas's growth is decelerating to mid-single digits; and its share gains are partly borrowed from Nike. I would not pin the case to anything above the 35th percentile within 18 months, because the company-specific route to a higher multiple (a visible footwear recovery) and the group route (Nike's stabilisation) are in tension: Nike's stabilisation is also adidas's main fundamental risk. The median (21.4x) is the 2028 target if the thesis broadens and the hedge roll is benign.

Counter-case. adidas offers the highest consensus EPS growth in its peer table at a multiple below the table's median, and the two-year median of 13.9x already includes the worst of the terrace narrative. If the market re-opens the "compounder" file, 21x to 24x (the 2019 and early-2025 levels) is where adidas traded last time, and a 19.7x fair multiple would prove conservative. What would change my view: a sportswear-group re-rating led by Nike's investor day being read as credible but slow, which favours the group's multiple without threatening adidas's share and would move my fair multiple toward the median; or lifestyle clearance into wholesale, which would move it to 16.3x or below.

Market view against mine. The median sell-side target of EUR 200 implies about 15x consensus FY2028 EPS, so the street sits implicitly below the 10th percentile, while the model's 28x sits above everyone. I sit between the street and the model, nearer the street.

#12 Total shareholder return: about +55% probability-weighted to March 2028, without the model's 28x

Conclusion: the return to March 2028 is built from about +18% from earnings (on forecasts below consensus), about 2% to 5% from dividends and anywhere from −15% to +66% from the multiple, depending on the band. The total is about +20% if the multiple holds, +50% to +80% at a turning-up multiple of 16.3x to 19.7x, and about +55% probability-weighted. The model's +183% at 28x is neither required nor assumed.

Score: 91, set by the Rater. About +55% maps to about 94, and the three-year check supports A. Moved down to 91 because the central case rests on a re-rating from 13x to 16-20x, the least certain lever, in a stock that has traded at 12-16x for eighteen months; only about +20% is earnings and dividends, and there is a fat lower tail (25% bear at -10%, tail -40%).

What the model says. At its guideline multiple of 28.03x, the model gives a total shareholder return of +182.9% to its 18-month column (31 March 2028; value per share EUR 478.26) and +234.8% to its three-year column (30 September 2029; EUR 566.05). The model's horizons are fixed columns, so they end on those dates, about 17 and 35 months from now.

The model's return needs two corrections. First, the model's earnings leg uses two-year-forward EPS at March 2028 of about 17.1, which carries the share-count artefact. On the corrected forecasts that EPS is about 15.5 (nine-twelfths of FY2029's 15.02 plus three-twelfths of FY2030's 16.76), against about 13.1 today, so the earnings leg is about +18% to March 2028, not +33%. To September 2029 it is about +37%, assuming FY2031 EPS grows 10%, which is outside the forecast range. Second, the model's multiple leg of +109% is the move from 13.4x to 28.03x and is the whole case in the model's version; in my version the multiple is the variable, not the given.

The return on my view, to 31 March 2028. The earnings leg is +18% in every case. Dividends add about 2% in cash by March 2028 (the FY2026 dividend of EUR 3.60, paid in May 2027), or about 5% if the May 2028 payment is counted, as the model counts it. The multiple leg ranges from −15% at the five-year low to +66% at the median, with the totals shown in the table. In the bear case (EPS 10% lower and an 11x multiple), the shares are worth about EUR 150, a return of about −10%. The tail case (Jefferies' and Morgan Stanley's bear values of EUR 100 to 105: no earnings growth from 2026 and a multiple below the five-year low) is about −40%. Weighting the 18-month outcomes at 25% bear (about −10%), 55% base at 16.3x to 19.7x (about +50% to +80%, centred on +65%) and 20% bull at the median (about +100%) gives an expected return of about +55%, with a floor near today's price if the multiple merely holds.

What drives the return, in order. The multiple is the largest lever and the least certain: each turn is worth about 9% of today's price. The earnings leg is the most certain part of the return: +18% to March 2028 on forecasts that sit below consensus and management, with about 60% of the 2027 bridge locked and about a fifth of EPS growth from the buyback. On its own, the earnings leg roughly matches the cost of holding the stock through the risk events. Dividends are small, a yield of about 2.1% rising to 2.6%. The sequence matters: the earnings leg is front-loaded (2027 EPS +25% on the clean base), the multiple leg is back-loaded (it needs the April and July 2027 results and a benign Nike), and the 2028 risks arrive after both.

So what for sizing. The case offers a low-teens to high-teens return from earnings alone if the multiple holds, a 50% to 80% return if the stock earns a turning-up multiple, and a tail of −10% to −40% if the lifestyle glide becomes a lurch. The case does not need the model's +183%. Richard should size the position on adidas's own range of outcomes rather than on sector beta, because two-thirds of the share-price variance is company-specific.

Counter-case. If the March 2027 guide trims sales and the April results show no hedge benefit in gross margin, the earnings leg shrinks to about +8% and the multiple leg turns negative, so the 18-month return is flat to negative. If Nike's investor day re-rates Nike and de-rates the rest of the sportswear group, the multiple leg is delayed by a year. What would change my view: a first-quarter 2027 gross margin above 53% (pull the multiple target toward the median); or lifestyle markdown breadth above 40% (cut it to the 10th percentile or below).

Market view against mine. The street's median target of EUR 200 (+16%) is roughly my "multiple holds, earnings deliver" case, and the model's EUR 478 is a mania case. My central value of EUR 250 to 305 sits between them.

#13 Summary conclusion: a predictability case at a floor multiple, with an asymmetric next six months

adidas is a good brand business run by an excellent operator, priced as if its earnings rose and fell with a sneaker fashion cycle that is visibly rolling over. adidas's earnings do not depend on that cycle to the degree the price implies. About 60% of the 2027 increase in operating profit is in the hands of the treasury, the sourcing team and a management that has beaten its initial profit guide four years running, and the buyback adds three points of EPS growth a year regardless. On our forecasts, which sit below consensus on revenue and below management on growth, EPS compounds at 14% to 16% a year to 2030, while the two-year-forward multiple of about 13x sits at the floor of a sportswear group that is itself at its floor. The case is therefore a composition case and a predictability case. The market will spend 2027 cutting adidas's revenue estimates and holding its profit estimates, and investors who understand why will be paid as the multiple moves from a bottoming band to a turning-up band.

The case has three honest weaknesses.

  • The demand leg is time-dated and partly borrowed from Nike. Nike's return from spring 2027 and the 2028 hedge roll make 2028 the year to doubt, and consensus for 2028 is more likely to be cut than raised.
  • The margin is managed. Upside to EPS is capped near the target, and the share price punishes any cost-led miss severely.
  • The foundations are adequate rather than excellent: returns below Nike's, pricing power based on brand heat, a thin bench and weak governance, in a sector that Viewforth's sector tilts rate Double Underweight.

Those weaknesses are why the fair multiple is the 35th percentile and not the median, and why the position should be sized on the stock's own range of outcomes.

The asymmetry of the next six months makes the situation attractive now. The two events the market fears, Nike's investor day on 16 and 17 November and the first guide under the new CFO on 10 March 2027, are both more likely to pass as non-events than to confirm the fear (a slow Nike plan; a sales-only trim with the margin held). The results that follow in April and July will then show gross margin rising on the hedge while the lifestyle cycle the market watches keeps declining. If the multiple merely holds, earnings and dividends return about 20% by March 2028; if the multiple reaches the band a turning-up stock deserves, the return is 50% to 80%. The downside to a fair trough is 15% to 25%, and it would need the lifestyle glide to become a lurch.

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 68, set by the Rater. The input forces are only a mild external positive (55) and a solid but maturing internal one (63), yet they reach profits with unusual certainty: about 60% of the 2027 bridge is locked by hedges, a falling contracted marketing load and buybacks, giving EPS of about 16% a year from the clean base (topic 6 A). Held below 75 because the demand force is decelerating and partly borrowed from Nike, most of the transformation is already in the numbers and the support fades in 2028.

Foundations' Robustness: 63, set by the Rater. A top-two global brand in a high-barrier oligopoly with an A-rated balance sheet and an operator who has beaten every initial guide since 2023 (topic 4 at 74) lifts it above typical, but quality (topic 3 at 62) is held down by brand-heat rather than structural pricing power, sub-Nike returns, unstable shares, weak governance, a thin bench and a history of fashion and geographic shocks. It lacks the stability that carried Richard's CVS to 80, so it sits near his Judges Scientific 60, a little higher for the delivery record.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 58, set by the Rater. The case fits a cause-for-concern-clearing setup in kind (a de-rated, medium-quality brand whose feared lifestyle rollover matters less to earnings than the price implies), but below Richard's 65-75 for a major concern clearing in a middling business. Today's problems blur the fit: footwear has been flat for two quarters, the terrace franchises are still declining, Europe is weak, and the concern (Nike re-arming) has to pass rather than clear, in a fashion-cyclical rather than steady business.

Case Riskiness: 57, set by the Rater. Over topic 9 (56): the margin line is locked and trackable, leverage is low and a multiple at the bottom of its range limits de-rating risk (the memo's fair trough is -15% to -25%), which Richard's CVS example counts in its favour. But the risks are not paper cuts: a single-brand fashion business with a footwear swing factor, a severe reaction function, a dated Nike event and correlated tariff and supply-chain tails keeps it near the middle.

Prices and dates. The share price of EUR 172.85 is the close on 2 November 2026 from the Master Dashboard. The Financial Analyst's model strikes its return at EUR 169.05 (3 November 2026). Money is in EUR millions unless stated.

Forecasts of record. The forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model after update 2 (revenue, EBITDA, EBIT and cash flow), read with the Analyst's cross-check EPS of EUR 9.70 for FY2026 (EUR 9.24 excluding the EUR 200m tariff refund and the EUR 100m fourth-quarter charge), 11.57 for FY2027, 13.42 for FY2028, 15.02 for FY2029 and 16.76 for FY2030. Nothing in the investment case rests on the model's own EPS line.

Two artefacts in the model's own EPS line. The model's own EPS line (14.31, 12.30, 14.38, 16.27 and 18.41 for FY2026 to FY2030) is overstated by two artefacts, both flagged to the Financial Analyst for correction; neither changes any forecast input. First, FactSet holds a zero EBITDA for the quarter to 30 September 2026, so the model's FY2026 EBITA (3,519) and EPS (14.31) are overstated by about EUR 990m and the related tax; the right figures are about 2,529 and 9.70. The same zero entry produces the 1.9x net debt to EBITDA shown in the FactSet block and the peer table; the correct figure is about 1.2x. Second, the model applies the 2026 buyback to a share count that already reflects it, and it converts future buybacks at today's share price rather than a rising one. Its FY2027 to FY2030 EPS, and its two-year-forward EPS at the return horizon, are therefore 6% to 9% too high (an implied buyback yield of 3.6% against the 3% the inputs intend). The model's cash flow from 2027 onward is correct; it is about EUR 90m a year below an earlier cross-check, which had double-counted lease interest.

Consensus. Consensus is the FactSet median of 3 November 2026 unless a chart's note says mean: EPS 9.64, 11.64, 13.64 and 15.06 for FY2026 to FY2029; revenue EUR 27.1bn, 29.2bn, 31.2bn and 33.6bn; EBIT 2,517, 2,894, 3,245 and 3,552.

Market data and the lifecycle. Market data and the letter grades come from the Master Dashboard. Its Phases page shows a two-year-forward P/E of 11.07x, which rests on the model's overstated EPS and should be read as about 13x. Its Stage 2 bucket reads "C_s1trans", a stage-one transition.

Charts. Charts marked “drawn from the figures in this memo” or “drawn with the chart kit” use only figures stated in the text. The default charts and tables carry their own source notes.

Grades. A 90 to 100, B 75 to 89, C 50 to 74, D 25 to 49, F 1 to 24. The Rater sets the scores.

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
